title: Press a guitar string at its middle
hook: An open guitar string hums at 110 Hz. Press it down at the middle: what comes out?

doesNotKnow: that a string's frequency is inversely proportional to its vibrating length

misconception: Shortening a string raises its pitch by some small, arbitrary amount.
objective: The learner can explain that a string's lowest vibration takes the shape of one loop over its free length, so halving the length halves the time per vibration and doubles the frequency (one octave).

claims.source: SI derived unit: 1 Hz = 1 s^-1 (BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed., Table 4).

claims.text: A guitar's open A string is tuned to 110 Hz, and a typical guitar's vibrating length (scale length) is about 0.65 m.
claims.source: Standard tuning A2 = 110 Hz (with A4 = 440 Hz, ISO 16:1975). Fender standard scale length 25.5 in = 0.648 m.

claims.text: A string's lowest note has frequency f = v / (2L): one loop over its free length L, with v the wave speed set by tension and mass per length.
claims.source: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, section 16.6 Standing Waves and Resonance (f_n = n v / 2L).

claims.text: With the same tension, pressing at the middle (0.325 m left) gives 220 Hz; a quarter along (0.4875 m) about 147 Hz; three quarters along (0.1625 m) 440 Hz.
claims.source: f = 110 x 0.65 / L: 0.325 -> 220.0, 0.4875 -> 146.7, 0.1625 -> 440.0 Hz (node; freq() in Demo.tsx). Pressing a real string stretches it slightly, raising the pitch a little; ignored.

claims.text: Doubling the frequency raises the note by one octave.
claims.source: An octave is a frequency ratio of 2:1 (any music acoustics text, e.g. Rossing, The Science of Sound, ch. 7).

claims.text: On the stage the vibration is slowed 55 times so it can be seen, and its width is exaggerated.
claims.source: Drawing choice: the loop pulses at f / 55 per second (110 Hz -> 2 per second). Labelled on stage.

recall.question: A string playing 200 Hz is shortened to a quarter of its length, same tension. Its note is about...
recall.why: Frequency goes as one over the vibrating length: a quarter of the length gives four times the frequency, two octaves up.
